strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_iclr2026_yao_medium_20260919T2254Z/scratch/10ebb009d91740f7a61396add39a8e0d/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses an important and relatively underexplored problem: high-level, algorithmic code optimization with language models.

The problem-oriented pairing idea is intuitive and practically motivated, and the qualitative examples clearly illustrate how solutions from different programmers can expose substantially different algorithms.
The experiments cover five model/scale combinations and report both BEST@1 and BEST@8. Improvements are large and broadly consistent, particularly for DeepSeek-Coder models.
Using unchanged validation/test sets and ensuring that programming problems do not cross dataset splits are good safeguards against direct problem leakage.
Evaluation includes functional correctness, optimization rate, speedup, deterministic gem5 measurements, merge-weight analysis, and a useful breakdown of failure modes.
weaknesses: The central causal comparison is substantially confounded. PIE-Problem changes not only programmer pairing but also the minimum training-pair improvement from 10% to 90%, the number and distribution of training problems and pairs, and the prompting/conditioning scheme. Consequently, the results do not establish that the problem-oriented perspective itself causes the gains. Matched controls such as user-oriented pairs filtered at 90%, problem-oriented pairs at 10%, size-matched datasets, and identical prompts are essential.

The model-merging results are insufficiently specified. The paper does not clearly state which merge coefficient produces each Table 3 result or whether coefficients were selected using validation data. Figure 5 appears to evaluate the full coefficient sweep on the test set, creating a serious risk of test-set model selection.

There are no uncertainty estimates, repeated fine-tuning runs, or significance tests. This is especially problematic because training and temperature-based decoding are stochastic and the 1,422 examples are clustered within only 80 underlying problems, so treating examples as independent would overstate effective sample size.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the availability claim: the manuscript provides no accessible artifact link and omits important details such as batch size, sequence length, random seeds, sampling implementation, exact checkpoints, merge settings, self-correction prompts, and gem5 CPU/cache configuration.

The speedup aggregate assigns a value of 1.0 to incorrect and slower outputs. This avoids penalizing regressions and conflates correctness with performance; conditional speedup distributions, regression rates, medians, and confidence intervals would provide a more faithful assessment.

The evaluation relies on finite competitive-programming test suites for semantic equivalence, without stronger differential testing, sanitizer checks, or analysis of undefined behavior. Aggressive algorithm rewriting can pass available tests while being incorrect on untested inputs.

The methodological novelty is limited: the main ingredients are a relatively straightforward re-pairing/filtering of an existing dataset and standard linear or spherical weight interpolation. Given the confounded comparison, the evidence is not yet strong enough to elevate this into a compelling top-tier contribution.

Comparisons are narrow and dated, lacking stronger contemporary code models and relevant alternatives such as matched-data training, mixed user/problem-oriented training, retrieval of other solutions, repair-plus-optimization pipelines, or candidate reranking under an equivalent compute budget.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and relatively underexplored problem: using code LLMs for high-level performance optimization rather than only functional code generation.

Constructing optimization pairs from different programmers solving the same problem is intuitive and could expose models to more substantial algorithmic changes than within-programmer revision histories.
The experiments cover two model families and several parameter scales, evaluate generated programs for correctness, compile with optimization enabled, and use gem5 to reduce timing noise.
The reported gains are large and consistent across the tested model sizes, suggesting that the proposed data may contain a useful training signal.
The comparison with prompting, self-correction, curriculum learning, and two merging procedures provides some empirical breadth.
weaknesses: The central comparison is severely confounded. PIE-User retains pairs with more than 10% improvement, whereas PIE-Problem requires more than 90%; the datasets also differ substantially in size, problem coverage, target distribution, and training prompts. Consequently, the results do not establish that cross-user, problem-oriented pairing—rather than selecting much larger speedups or another changed factor—causes the gains. Controlled variants matching pair count, problems, speedup distribution, and prompting are essential.

The paper lacks basic ablations needed to validate the data-construction claim: same-user pairs at the 90% threshold, cross-user pairs at the 10% threshold, matched subsets, randomly paired or fastest-target alternatives, and mixtures of user- and problem-oriented examples. It also does not compare model merging against the natural baseline of jointly training on the two datasets.

The model-merging contribution is technically incremental and underspecified. Linear interpolation and SLERP are established methods, while the paper provides little explanation for why parameter averaging should combine the claimed capabilities. It is unclear how merge weights were selected, whether Figure 5 uses the test set for tuning, and whether all reported results use validation-selected hyperparameters. Test-set selection would materially invalidate the headline numbers.

The evaluation reports arithmetic mean speedup after assigning a value of 1.0 to incorrect and slower outputs. This clipping hides regressions, while the arithmetic mean can be dominated by a few extreme speedups. Per-problem aggregation, distributions, geometric means, confidence intervals, significance tests, and total-runtime measures are absent.

Correctness is inferred solely from finite test suites, despite the method encouraging major algorithmic rewrites. No analysis estimates false acceptance from inadequate tests, and no formal, fuzzing-based, or additional hidden-test validation is provided. BEST@8 furthermore uses an oracle that executes all candidates on the evaluation tests, so its practical assumptions and risk of test-specific selection need clearer treatment.

The 1,422 test pairs come from only 80 problems, but results are aggregated at the pair level without clarifying duplicate source programs or dependence among pairs. This can overweight particular problems and makes the effective sample size and generalization evidence unclear.

The claim that problem-oriented pairs predominantly represent global algorithmic optimization is weakly supported. The human analysis covers only 100 pairs and provides no annotator count, protocol, blinding, inter-annotator agreement, or uncertainty. The authors acknowledge that GPT-4 tends to mistake large textual changes for algorithmic improvements, undermining the much larger automated analysis.

Several interpretations are speculative rather than experimentally demonstrated, including the proposed relationship between code comprehension and optimization, the explanation for curriculum learning's failure, and the claim that model merging avoids 'fixed thinking patterns.' No mechanistic or output-level analysis supports these statements.

Reproducibility is insufficient for the headline results: no accessible artifact link is given despite the availability claim, and important details such as exact dataset-generation and deduplication procedures, gem5 configuration, sampling seeds, merge implementation and weights, decoding limits, and the full self-correction protocol are missing.

The scope is narrow—C++ competitive-programming submissions from one source—and the paper does not evaluate transfer to real repositories, maintainability, memory use, portability, or realistic performance workloads. The manuscript also omits meaningful discussion of licensing, attribution, resource costs, and safe execution of generated or untrusted code.

Overall, the idea is promising and the numerical results are notable, but the uncontrolled dataset comparison and evaluation/tuning ambiguities prevent the main causal claim from being established at a top-tier standard. strengths: The paper identifies an intuitive and practically meaningful limitation of user-trajectory optimization data: iterative submissions from one programmer tend to encode local edits, whereas solutions from different programmers expose alternative algorithms and data structures.

The proposed PIE-Problem construction is simple but potentially useful. Problem-level train/validation/test separation is reported, and the manual and GPT-4 analyses provide supporting evidence that the reconstructed pairs contain substantially more global algorithmic changes.

The empirical gains are large and broadly consistent across CodeLlama and DeepSeek-Coder model families and multiple parameter scales. The evaluation includes both BEST@1 and BEST@8, correctness, optimization rate, and speedup on a reasonably large 1,422-example test set.

Using gem5, many test cases per problem, GCC -O3, and a strict all-tests correctness criterion makes the execution-time evaluation more credible and reproducible than measurements on uncontrolled shared hardware.
The merge-weight study, failure analysis, qualitative examples, and comparisons with self-correction and curriculum learning help explain the observed correctness-versus-aggressiveness tradeoff.
weaknesses: The central comparison does not isolate the effect of the claimed problem-oriented perspective. PIE-User retains pairs with more than 10% improvement and uses performance-conditioned prompts, whereas PIE-Problem requires more than 90% improvement and uses a different prompt. Dataset size, target speedup, sampling, and training format all change simultaneously. Controlled variants matching these factors are needed before attributing the gains specifically to cross-user pairing.

PIE-Problem pairs independently written solutions rather than demonstrated edits of the source program. This may train wholesale solution replacement rather than code optimization, and the paper does not assess edit magnitude, preservation of interfaces or coding constraints, or performance on realistic non-competitive-programming code.

The model-merging evidence lacks important controls and methodological details. The final interpolation coefficient and whether it was selected exclusively on validation data are unclear; sweeping it on the test set would introduce test-selection bias. Joint or mixed-dataset training, adapter composition, and inference-time selection between the two specialized models are also missing baselines.

Reported results have no confidence intervals, repeated fine-tuning runs, or statistical tests. Mean speedup can be dominated by a small number of extreme improvements, so medians, distributions, and per-problem paired analyses would materially strengthen the evidence.

Functional equivalence is approximated by a fixed test suite. Given BEST@8 selection and the high rate of semantically incorrect outputs, additional held-out or generated tests are important to quantify test-suite overfitting.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the availability claim: the manuscript provides limited dataset-construction and model-merging details, does not identify the released repository, and omits information such as random seeds, batching, sequence length, coefficient selection, and computational cost. Overall, the results are promising, but these confounds keep the main causal claim slightly below the acceptance bar.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and comparatively underexplored problem: high-level, execution-time optimization of code using LLMs.

Reconstructing training pairs across programmers is intuitive and potentially useful because it exposes models to qualitatively different algorithms rather than only incremental edits by one programmer.

The main empirical improvements are large and broadly consistent across several model families and parameter scales. The evaluation also includes correctness, optimization rate, and speedup rather than speed alone.
Problem-level separation between training, validation, and test sets is an important safeguard against direct problem leakage.

Using the original correct program as an execution oracle is a sensible application of differential testing. Anchor verification consistently outperforms self-debugging and direct synthetic-test generation across the reported refinement models.
The paper provides prompts, core training settings, dataset statistics, data-scaling experiments, and illustrative case studies.
weaknesses: The central PIE-versus-PCO comparison is seriously confounded. PCO pairs are selected from a much larger combinatorial pool using the top speedups, whereas PIE consists of sequential within-user pairs. The datasets are matched only in pair count, not in source runtime, target runtime, speedup distribution, code length, target reuse, or effective number of unique programs. Consequently, the results do not establish that cross-programmer pairing or algorithmic diversity causes the gains; they may primarily reflect selecting much stronger targets.

Essential ablations are missing: within-user all-pairs with the same speedup selection, cross-user pairs matched by speedup, random rather than top-ranked PCO pairs, deduplicated source/target programs, and controls for repeated fast targets. These are necessary to isolate the proposed perspective from selection and duplication effects.

The effective evaluation contains only 41 unique problems, although results are aggregated over 978 correlated program pairs. There are no per-problem results, confidence intervals, significance tests, or multi-seed fine-tuning results, so the robustness of the large reported gains is unclear.

BEST@8 uses an oracle that selects the fastest candidate passing every evaluation test. This reuses the correctness test suite for selection and is not a realistic deployable procedure; it should be clearly treated as an oracle upper bound and supplemented with selection using only validation-generated tests.

Correctness is defined solely by passing available tests, which may not establish semantic equivalence. This is particularly concerning for anchor verification, where only three LLM-generated inputs drive repair. There is no analysis using stronger fuzzing, held-out adversarial tests, or formal equivalence checks.

Runtime evaluation is underspecified. The paper names gem5 and compiler settings but omits simulator configuration, input/workload construction, timing repetitions, variance, timeout handling, and sensitivity to architecture. These omissions weaken the credibility and reproducibility of the speedup claims.

The supporting analyses are not rigorous enough to validate the proposed explanation. CFG construction and graph-edit costs are unspecified; t-SNE is used as qualitative evidence without quantitative diversity measures; and the 100-example human study lacks annotation instructions, number of annotators, agreement, uncertainty, and blinding.

Anchor verification is closely related to standard differential testing with a reference implementation, making its novelty modest. Its comparisons are also limited to one iteration and do not control for inference cost, token budget, number of executions, or additional repair baselines.

Reproducibility details remain incomplete, including batch size, sequence length, sampling and filtering algorithms, random seeds, exact checkpoints, inference limits, and full benchmark construction. The claimed public release is not sufficient to resolve these omissions within the manuscript.

The paper does not discuss dataset licensing, the exposure of programmer identifiers in examples, or risks associated with automatically deploying optimized but insufficiently verified code. Overall, the empirical signal is promising, but the main causal claim and headline improvements are not supported by a sufficiently controlled evaluation for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and relatively underexplored problem: using code LLMs for high-level runtime optimization rather than merely generating functionally correct code.

The problem-oriented construction is intuitive and potentially useful: solutions from different programmers can expose substantially different algorithms that a single-user edit trajectory may not contain.

The experiments cover several model families and sizes and report complementary metrics for optimization rate, speedup, and correctness. The problem-disjoint train/validation/test split and use of GCC -O3 with gem5 are positive design choices.

The reported BEST@1 improvements are large and broadly consistent across models. The structural analysis, manual optimization-type analysis, and training-data percentage study provide some evidence beyond a single headline result.

Using the original correct program as an execution oracle is sensible for optimization. Anchor verification consistently improves correctness over self-debugging and direct test generation across three refinement models.
weaknesses: The central PIE-versus-PCO comparison is seriously confounded. PCO retains the highest-speedup cross-user pairs for each problem, while PIE consists of the original within-user pairs. Matching only the number of pairs does not control target speedup, source difficulty, edit distance, target-solution quality, or algorithm distribution. Consequently, the large gains cannot be attributed specifically to the problem-oriented perspective. Essential controls include top-speedup within-user pairs and cross-user pairs matched on runtime ratios and other pair properties.

The PCO construction is internally unclear. The text alternates between adjacent pairs along a runtime-sorted trajectory, examples containing apparently non-adjacent pairs, and a formula counting all pairwise combinations. Runtime thresholds, tie handling, deduplication, filtering, and the exact selection algorithm are not specified adequately, materially limiting reproducibility.

BEST@8 appears to select the fastest candidate that passes all benchmark test cases. If these are also the cases used to report correctness, this is test-set oracle selection and substantially overstates deployable performance. Candidate selection and final evaluation require disjoint tests. Although BEST@1 results avoid some of this issue, the paper prominently emphasizes BEST@8.

The evaluation provides no repeated-run variation, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Arithmetic mean speedup can be dominated by a few extreme cases; per-problem distributions, medians or geometric means, and repeated measurements are needed to establish robustness.

Functional equivalence is inferred solely from passing a finite competitive-programming test suite. This is particularly risky because PCO encourages major algorithmic rewrites. Stronger independent fuzzing, differential testing, or formal checks are needed, together with an analysis of false positives permitted by the benchmark tests.

Anchor verification is essentially differential testing against a reference implementation, so its conceptual novelty is limited. The baselines are weak: direct test generation is denied access to the reliable output oracle, and the paper omits comparisons with standard oracle-based random, boundary, coverage-guided, or fuzz-generated inputs. There are also no ablations over input-generation strategy, number of tests, or refinement iterations.

The anchor method's extra computational cost is not reported. Executing the deliberately slow reference program, invoking a powerful external LLM, and performing compilation and refinement may be expensive; token, wall-clock, and execution costs are necessary for a practical optimization claim.

Several supporting analyses are not rigorous enough. The t-SNE visualization is not quantitative evidence of semantic diversity; CFG edit-distance computation and normalization are underspecified; and the 100-example human study lacks annotator counts, agreement statistics, and uncertainty.

The empirical scope is narrow: C++ competitive-programming submissions from one source. BEST@1 correctness remains only 74.54% even after the strongest refinement, making claims about practicability and ensuring correctness too strong. Generalization to real repositories, APIs, memory behavior, nondeterminism, and maintainability is not evaluated.

Important implementation details such as batch size, context length, decoding limits, seeds, runtime-measurement repetitions, timeouts, and complete data-generation scripts are missing from the manuscript. Overall, the ideas are promising, but the uncontrolled central comparison and evaluation issues prevent the evidence from supporting the main claims at a top-tier standard.

strengths: Addresses an important and comparatively underexplored problem: high-level, algorithmic optimization of functionally correct code rather than compiler-level transformations or code generation alone.

The problem-oriented pairing strategy is intuitive and practically useful. It leverages solutions from multiple programmers and produces substantially more structurally diverse optimization examples than same-user submission trajectories.

The main empirical improvements are large and consistent across five model configurations: PCO training improves optimization rate, speedup, and often correctness over equal-sized PIE training sets. Problem-level separation between training, validation, and test sets reduces direct leakage concerns.

Anchor verification makes effective use of a property specific to optimization: the original slow program can serve as an execution oracle. Across three refinement models, it consistently outperforms self-debugging and direct LLM-generated tests.

The evaluation includes BEST@1 and BEST@8 results, correctness and efficiency metrics, an O3-compiled gem5 setup, a data-efficiency study, multiple model families and scales, and illustrative case studies.
weaknesses: The central comparison does not cleanly isolate the benefit of crossing user boundaries. PCO retains the highest-speedup pairs, whereas PIE consists of chronological same-user pairs; consequently, target speedup, edit magnitude, and pair difficulty are confounded with user diversity. Controls matching the speedup/edit-distance distributions, or comparing within-user and cross-user pairs under identical sampling, are needed.

Runtime evaluation lacks uncertainty estimates, repeated-run details, simulator configuration, and significance tests. Arithmetic-mean speedup can be dominated by outliers, while assigning a speedup of 1 to incorrect or slower outputs obscures the underlying distribution. BEST@8 also uses the full correctness test suite to select candidates, making it partly oracle-assisted.

Anchor verification is closely related to standard differential testing with a reference implementation, so its conceptual novelty is moderate. Comparisons omit stronger testing baselines such as fuzzing, coverage-guided input generation, mutation testing, or hybrid random-plus-LLM testing; the paper also does not report inference and execution costs.

Several supporting analyses are insufficiently rigorous: the t-SNE visualization cannot establish semantic diversity, CFG/GED construction and normalization are underspecified, and the 100-example human study reports neither annotator count nor inter-annotator agreement. The paper acknowledges that GPT-4 tends to conflate large edits with algorithmic changes.

Reproducibility details remain incomplete, including the exact pair-selection algorithm, handling of timing noise and ties, runtime repetitions and timeouts, sequence lengths, batch sizes, random seeds, and full decoding/refinement budgets.

The evidence is restricted to accepted competitive-programming C++ submissions whose original programs are assumed correct. Generalization to real repositories, stateful or nondeterministic programs, other languages, memory optimization, and imperfect reference implementations is not established.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and relatively underexplored problem: improving the runtime of functionally correct programs using code LLMs.

The problem-oriented construction is simple and practically meaningful. Problem-disjoint train/validation/test splits reduce direct leakage, and the reported gains over the original user-oriented PIE construction are large and consistent across five model configurations.

The evaluation is unusually broad, including BEST@k scaling, a random-pair ablation, data-size and GED analyses, two programming languages, several refinement backbones, failure analysis, and a small physical-hardware validation.

Using the original correct program as an execution oracle is a sensible way to avoid hallucinated expected outputs. Anchor verification consistently outperforms self-debugging and direct test generation in the reported experiments.
The manuscript is generally clear, and it provides prompts, core training hyperparameters, dataset statistics, and computational-cost measurements.
weaknesses: The claimed novelty of anchor verification is limited: executing a reference implementation as an oracle is essentially differential/regression testing. The comparison omits stronger testing and program-repair baselines such as coverage-guided input generation, fuzzing, property-based testing, and execution-aware code-debugging methods, making it difficult to establish the contribution beyond a straightforward oracle-testing baseline.

The causal claim that the cross-user perspective itself produces the gain remains undercontrolled. PCO-Random and PIE match pair counts and problems but not source-runtime, target-runtime, speedup, structural-distance, target-frequency, or duplicate-code distributions. Random sampling from a combinatorially larger cross-user pool therefore changes substantially more than perspective. A distribution-matched comparison is needed.

The data-scarcity argument counts a quadratic number of pairings as if they were independent supervision, although these pairs heavily reuse the same programs and can create near duplicates. The experiments keep PCO and PIE at the same size and thus do not actually validate the claimed scaling advantage.

Runtime evaluation lacks statistical rigor. Results are reported without repeated training or decoding seeds, confidence intervals, timing variance, or robustness to measurement noise. Arithmetic mean speedup can also be dominated by a few extreme cases; medians, geometric means, and per-problem distributions would be informative.

BEST@k uses an oracle that selects the fastest candidate passing the benchmark test suite. This is useful as an upper-bound analysis but is not generally deployable when hidden correctness tests are unavailable, so the strong BEST@8 numbers overstate practical performance. Even BEST@1 correctness is defined only by finite benchmark tests rather than semantic equivalence.

The physical-hardware study covers only 20 selected pairs, while the displayed table aggregates them into seven categories without uncertainty estimates or per-instance results. This is insufficient to substantiate broad real-world-performance claims.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: no artifact or release link is provided, and important details such as exact pair-generation and deduplication rules, gem5 configuration, timing protocol, preprocessing, random seeds, and the test suites used for correctness are missing.

The paper discusses generalization to real software largely speculatively. Competitive-programming solutions to a shared specification differ substantially from repository-scale optimization involving APIs, state, concurrency, build systems, and side effects. Executing generated or submitted programs also raises sandboxing and security concerns that are not meaningfully addressed.

strengths: The paper studies an important and relatively underexplored problem: improving algorithmic execution time while preserving program behavior.
Constructing training pairs from solutions by different programmers is intuitive, and the reported gains over same-user PIE pairs are large and consistent across several model families and sizes.

The evaluation includes useful extensions and ablations, including random versus top-speedup PCO sampling, GED-stratified subsets, BEST@k scaling, Python experiments, refinement backbones, iteration counts, failure analysis, and limited physical-hardware validation.

The split by problem ID avoids the most direct form of train-test leakage, and evaluation above GCC -O3 is appropriate.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is limited. PCO is principally a re-pairing and selection scheme over existing accepted submissions, while anchor verification is differential testing against a trusted reference implementation. The paper does not adequately distinguish the latter from established oracle-based testing, fuzzing, and execution-guided repair.

The central causal claim about the “problem-oriented perspective” is not cleanly established. PCO-Random and PIE differ not only in programmer identity but also in edit distance, runtime-gap distribution, chronological relation, target-solution frequency, and likely code-length and algorithm distributions. Matching only the number of pairs and problems does not isolate perspective from these confounders.

The claimed alleviation of data scarcity is overstated: forming a combinatorial number of pairs from the same finite set of programs does not create comparably independent information. Moreover, the experiments deliberately hold the training set at 78K pairs, so the proposed scaling advantage is not actually evaluated.

The evaluation has only 41 unique C++ test problems, despite reporting results over 978 highly correlated program instances. Results are not aggregated per problem, and no confidence intervals, seed variance, significance tests, or robustness to alternative splits are provided. Consequently, the precision and generality implied by the tables are unsupported.

The speedup metric averages raw ratios and can be dominated by a few extreme improvements. The paper provides neither distributions nor geometric means, medians, tail behavior, or per-problem results. Timing methodology also omits important details such as repetitions, warm-up, variance, simulator configuration, and timeout handling.

BEST@k selects the fastest candidate that passes all benchmark tests, effectively granting an oracle test-suite-based selector. This makes the large BEST@8 gains difficult to interpret as a deployable result, especially without comparisons to selectors operating only on generated or public tests.

Calling anchor-generated tests “verified” risks conflating correct labels with adequate behavioral coverage. Only three LLM-generated inputs are used, so agreement with the slow program does not establish semantic equivalence. Even after five refinement iterations, roughly 21% of outputs remain incorrect, which substantially limits the claimed practicability.

The anchor-verification baselines are weak. There are no comparisons with coverage-guided or mutation-based fuzzing, property-based testing, stronger differential-testing input generators, search-based repair, or budget-matched execution-guided methods. The comparison also does not rigorously control token, query, or wall-clock budgets.

The physical-hardware study is too small and opaque to support real-world claims: only 20 pairs are sampled, Table 13 reports seven category-level values without individual observations or uncertainty, and it is unclear how the stated Pearson correlation was calculated. Competitive-programming programs are also far removed from the large, stateful, dependency-heavy systems discussed in the generalizability section.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the scale of the empirical claims. There is no code or dataset release statement, and key details are missing, including random seeds, exact API model snapshots, complete decoding settings, batch/context configurations, test-suite sizes, pair filters, sandbox behavior, and raw timing measurements.

The work does not discuss the security implications of compiling and executing model-generated code, nor dataset licensing and provenance considerations. The paper also contains numerous grammatical, typographical, and typesetting issues that reduce clarity.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and relatively underexplored problem: high-level, algorithmic code optimization with LLMs while preserving functional correctness.

The problem-oriented construction is simple but meaningful. Pairing solutions across programmers plausibly exposes models to larger algorithmic transformations than same-user revision trajectories, and the reported gains are large and consistent across several model families and sizes.

The evaluation is unusually broad: it includes C/C++ and Python, BEST@1 and BEST@8, multiple dataset fractions, a random-pair control, GED-stratified subsets, several refinement backbones, iteration-count studies, failure analysis, and limited validation on physical hardware.

The anchor-verification framework makes effective use of a property specific to optimization: the original program can serve as an executable reference oracle. Results consistently improve over self-debugging and direct test generation, including substantial correctness gains.

The paper is well organized, provides concrete examples, reports training configurations and compute, and separates optimization rate, correctness, and speedup rather than collapsing them into one outcome.
weaknesses: The claimed isolation of the problem-oriented perspective is incomplete. PCO-Random matches PIE in pair count and problems, but not necessarily in speedup distribution, source/target reuse, runtime gap, structural distance, or number of unique programs. Thus it does not establish that perspective alone, rather than changed pair statistics, causes the gain. A matched-pair control is needed.

Anchor verification is closely related to standard differential testing and regression-oracle techniques, making its conceptual novelty moderate. Comparisons omit stronger testing baselines such as randomized or coverage-guided differential testing, mutation-guided input generation, and combinations of generated and existing tests.

Correctness is defined by passing finite benchmark test suites, while both training labels and evaluation rely on accepted competitive-programming submissions. The paper does not quantify test-suite strength, undefined-behavior risks, or false equivalence, so claims such as a gold-standard anchor and verified test cases are stronger than the evidence supports.

BEST@k appears to select the fastest candidate that passes all evaluation tests, which uses an oracle unavailable in realistic deployment and can overfit selection to the benchmark suite. BEST@1 results remain valuable, but BEST@8 should be labeled as oracle selection or evaluated with separate selection and held-out test sets.

Runtime reporting lacks uncertainty estimates, repeated-run details for the main experiments, and robust aggregate statistics. Arithmetic mean speedup can be dominated by a few extreme improvements; per-problem distributions, confidence intervals, and median or geometric-mean results would make the evidence more convincing.

The physical-hardware validation is limited to 20 pairs, and the relationship between those samples and the seven rows in the reported table is unclear. The paper also does not provide an explicit artifact or release commitment for PCO, code, test-generation infrastructure, or model adapters, limiting reproducibility.
